messages.content: Write a page comparing a managed database service with running your own, for a technical audience choosing between them. Around 250 words.

# Managed database or your own?

Both can be reliable. The choice is really about where your engineering hours go, and how much control you need over the parts that break.

A managed service sells you an operational floor: backups that restore, point-in-time recovery, failover, patching, and someone else's pager at 3am. You pay in three currencies. Money, usually two to four times raw compute. Control, in that you get the versions, extensions and parameters the vendor supports and nothing else. And a ceiling on debugging: when the provider's storage layer stalls, you open a ticket and wait.

Self-hosting hands all of that back. Pick your Postgres version, load any extension, tune the page cache, read the kernel log when p99 latency doubles. In exchange, the operational floor is yours to build and keep standing: verified backups, replica promotion, connection pooling, rehearsed upgrades, and enough people to staff a rotation.

A rough rule. Self-host when the database is the product, or when your bill exceeds the salary of the SRE you would otherwise hire. Under a few hundred gigabytes with a handful of engineers, managed wins, mostly because restore drills are the sort of thing small teams plan and never run.

Two traps. Teams compare the managed bill against server cost and forget the salary line on the other side. And they treat the decision as permanent when it is only expensive in one direction: leaving a managed service is much harder than joining one, so the migration worth costing out in advance is the exit, not the entry.

---

~250 words. I ran it through this repo's `slopwatch` ruleset before handing it over — it passes the live gate with no blocking issues. Not written to a file; say the word if you want it saved somewhere.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
# Managed database or your own?

Reliability is reachable either way. The real question is where your engineering hours go, and how deep you are allowed to dig when something breaks.

What a managed service sells is an operational floor. Backups that actually restore, point-in-time recovery, failover, patching, and a pager that belongs to someone else at 3am. You pay for that floor three times over. In money, usually two to four times raw compute. In control, since you get the versions, extensions and parameters the vendor happens to support. And in depth, because when the provider's storage layer stalls, your only move is a ticket and a wait.

Run it yourself and all of that comes back. Choose the Postgres version, load whatever extension you like, tune the page cache, read the kernel log when p99 latency doubles. The bill is that the operational floor is now yours to build and keep standing. Verified backups, replica promotion, connection pooling, rehearsed upgrades, and enough people to fill a rotation.

Rough rule. Run your own when the database is the product, or when the managed bill passes the salary of the SRE you would hire instead. Under a few hundred gigabytes with a handful of engineers, managed wins, largely because restore drills are the sort of thing small teams schedule and never actually run.

Two traps. Teams weigh the managed bill against server cost and quietly drop the salary line. And they treat the call as permanent when it is only costly in one direction. Joining a managed service is easy, leaving is not, so the migration to price out ahead of time is the exit.
